title: Star and mesh topologies
specPoints: How each works, advantages and disadvantages of each
Drawing a topology and choosing one for a given scenario
learn: Draw a star topology and a mesh topology (full and partial) with correct labels
Describe how data travels in each topology
Give at least three advantages and two disadvantages of each
Calculate the number of links in a full mesh of n devices using n(n−1)/2
Recommend a topology for a scenario and justify it
hook: Six of you, stand in a circle. Pass a ball to anyone, but only through me in the middle. Now I sit down. What happens? Nothing moves. Reset: this time, every one of you holds a string to every other person. I leave; nothing changes. Count the strings. Fifteen, for six people. That is the whole lesson: one hub that is cheap but critical, or lots of links that are expensive but unbreakable.

video.title: Star and mesh: one hub or many links
video.brief: 4 minutes. Draw a star: a switch in the centre, six devices on their own cables. Send a packet from A to D: it goes A to switch to D, nothing else hears it. Cut cable B: only B drops off. Then the switch fails: every link dies at once. Redraw as a full mesh: every device cabled to every other; count links with the formula n(n-1)/2 appearing on screen for n = 4, 6, 10. Send A to D directly; cut two links and show the packet re-routing. Then thin it to a partial mesh: some links removed, still more than one route. Finish with wireless mesh: a home with three mesh Wi-Fi nodes, and a city sensor network, as examples where mesh is used in practice.

p: In a **star** topology every device has its own cable to a **central device**, usually a **switch** (older networks used a hub). All data goes through the centre. If A sends to D, the frame goes A to switch to D; the switch reads the MAC address and forwards it only to D's port. Almost every school and office LAN is a star.
explain.code:
[ PC ]
              |
[ PC ]---[ SWITCH ]---[ Printer ]
              |
           [ Server ]

Every device has ONE cable to the centre.
A to Server: A -> switch -> Server

list: **Advantage**: if one cable or device fails, only that device is affected; the rest keep working.
**Advantage**: easy to add a device: plug a new cable into the switch.
**Advantage**: fast and few collisions, because the switch sends each frame only to the right port.
**Advantage**: easy to find faults: one cable per device.
**Disadvantage**: if the **central switch fails, the whole network stops**: a single point of failure.
**Disadvantage**: needs a lot of cable and a switch, so it costs more than a single shared cable would.
**Disadvantage**: performance depends on the switch; a cheap or overloaded switch is the bottleneck.

p: In a **mesh** topology devices are connected to **each other**, not to a centre. In a **full mesh** every device is directly linked to every other device. In a **partial mesh** most devices have several links, but not to everyone. Data can take **many routes**: if one link is busy or broken, it goes another way. Each device helps forward data for the others.

Mesh is used where reliability matters more than cost: the backbone of the internet, military and emergency networks, and, increasingly, **wireless mesh** systems such as home Wi-Fi with several nodes or smart-city sensor networks, where links are radio rather than cable.
explain.code:
Full mesh (4 devices, 6 links):      Partial mesh (4 devices, 4 links):

   A -------- B                         A -------- B
   | \      / |                         |          |
   |   \  /   |                         |          |
   |   /  \   |                         |          |
   | /      \ |                         |          |
   C -------- D                         C -------- D

Every pair linked directly.           Still a second route from A to D (via B or C).

list: **Advantage**: **no single point of failure**: if one link or node fails, data takes another route.
**Advantage**: data can travel by many paths at once, so heavy traffic is spread and there is less congestion.
**Advantage**: new nodes can be added and the network keeps working; in wireless mesh, each node extends the range.
**Disadvantage**: a wired full mesh needs a huge number of cables and ports, so it is **expensive** and impractical for many devices.
**Disadvantage**: complex to set up and manage: routing must be worked out, and faults are harder to trace.
**Disadvantage**: in wireless mesh, every node forwards traffic for others, so nodes need more processing and power.

p: In a full mesh with **n** devices, every device links to the other n−1, but each link is shared by two devices, so the number of links is **n(n−1)/2**. The numbers show why wired full mesh does not scale.

Ask two questions. **Does a stop matter?** A classroom losing its network for an hour is annoying; a hospital, a stock exchange or an emergency service cannot stop, so mesh (or at least extra links) is justified. **How many devices and how much money?** Thirty PCs on a budget is a star. The exam wants the choice plus reasons that quote the scenario: 'because the clinic cannot lose access to patient records' or 'because the office has 25 computers and a limited budget'.
One switch in the middle. Every device has its own cable to it.
Data goes device, switch, device.
Good: one broken cable only affects one device. Easy to add devices. Fast.
Bad: if the switch breaks, everything stops. Needs lots of cable.
Devices connect to each other. No middle.
Full mesh: every device links to every other device.
Partial mesh: most devices have several links, not all.
Good: if one link breaks, data goes another way. No single point of failure.
Bad: lots of cables. Expensive. Hard to set up.
Full mesh links = n(n−1)/2.
6 devices: 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15 links.
Star with 6 devices: 6 cables.

list: Must never stop (hospital, emergency services): mesh.
Office or school on a budget: star.

keyterms.def: The layout of how devices in a network are connected.
A layout where every device connects by its own cable to a central switch or hub.
A layout where devices connect directly to other devices, giving more than one route for data.
A mesh where every device is directly connected to every other device.
A mesh where devices have several connections but not to every other device.
One component whose failure stops the whole network, such as the switch in a star.
Any device connected to a network.

try.title: 1. Draw both
p: Draw, label and compare. Use a ruler; examiners cannot give marks for a diagram they cannot read.
steps: Star: one switch, five devices (two PCs, a laptop, a printer, a server). Label the central device. Draw an arrow showing the path from a PC to the printer.
Full mesh: five devices, every pair connected. Count the links and check with n(n−1)/2.
Partial mesh: same five devices, remove links until every device still has at least two routes to every other. How few links can you keep?
Under each drawing write one sentence: what happens if the busiest device fails.

try.title: 2. How many cables?
p: Run the program. Then: at what number of devices does a full mesh need more than 1000 cables? Add a line that prints the cost difference if each cable costs 15 pounds.

try.title: 3. Break it
p: Use string and six students, as in the hook. Time how long each test takes to 'deliver' a message card from student 1 to student 4.
steps: Star round: one student is the switch. Deliver. Then the switch sits down. Deliver again.
Mesh round: every student holds string to every other. Deliver. Cut (drop) two strings. Deliver again.
Record: which topology kept working? How many strings did the mesh need? Who got tired of holding strings?

try.title: 4. Topology section
instructions: Open the topology activities. Do the star vs mesh sort and the labelling task.
Note one advantage or disadvantage the page gives that you had not written down.

try.title: 5. Choose and justify
p: For each scenario, pick star, full mesh or partial mesh. Two sentences each, using the scenario's words.
steps: A primary school with 60 computers in six classrooms and a tight budget.
The control network for an air traffic control tower.
A large house where Wi-Fi from one router does not reach the garden room; the owner buys three wireless 'mesh' nodes.
A hospital operating theatre where monitors must never lose connection to the records system.
A pop-up shop with four tablets for one weekend.

check.q: In a star topology, all data passes through:
The main disadvantage of a star topology is:
opts: If the central device fails the whole network stops
check.fb: The switch is the single point of failure.

check.q: In a full mesh, how many links join 8 devices?
The main advantage of a mesh topology is:
opts: There are many routes, so no single point of failure

check.q: Which is TRUE of a partial mesh?
opts: Every device links to every other
Devices link to a central hub
Most devices have several links but not to every device
check.fb: Some links removed, but more than one route remains.

exam.q: Draw a diagram of a **star** topology with one switch and four computers. Label the switch.
model: Central device drawn and labelled switch (1); four computers each connected by a separate line to the switch only, with no links between computers (1).
exam.commentary: Lose the second mark by joining computers to each other or drawing a 'daisy chain'. Lose the first by leaving the centre unlabelled or labelling it 'router'. Use a ruler; a clear diagram is quick marks.

exam.q: Describe **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of a mesh topology compared with a star topology.
model: Advantage: there are multiple routes between devices (1), so if one link or device fails data can still be delivered, whereas in a star the failure of the switch stops everything (1). Disadvantage: many more cables/connections are needed (1), so it is more expensive and harder to set up and manage than a star (1).
exam.commentary: 'Describe' here wants the point and what follows from it. 'More reliable' alone is one mark; 'more reliable because data can take another route if a link fails' is two. Mentioning the star in each answer is what makes it a comparison.

exam.q: A dental surgery has eight computers that must all access patient records on a server. The practice manager is concerned about reliability but has a limited budget. Recommend a topology and justify your recommendation.
model: Star (1) with the server and computers connected to a central switch. Justification: only nine cables and one switch are needed, which suits the limited budget (1); if one computer's cable fails the rest keep working, which addresses reliability for most faults (1); a full mesh of nine devices would need 36 links, which is far too expensive for a small surgery (1). Accept a partial mesh or a star with a spare/backup switch if argued from the reliability concern.
exam.commentary: Both scenario clues are in the question: 'reliability' and 'limited budget'. A full-marks answer deals with both and shows it knows the star's weak point (the switch) and why it is acceptable here. Calculating 36 mesh links is a strong, concrete justification.

home: Draw the topology of a network you know (home, school, a shop) and label it star, mesh or partial mesh. Then work out, with the formula, how many cables a full mesh of your household's devices would need.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 6 · explain 10 · try 28 · check 5 · exam 8 · homework 3
misconceptions: Calling the central device a router. In a LAN star it is a switch (or a hub in older networks). The router is at the edge.
Drawing a 'star' where devices are also linked to each other, or a ring. Star = spokes only.
'Mesh is always wireless' or 'mesh is always wired'. Both exist; the spec cares about the layout, not the medium.
Dividing n(n−1) by 2 is forgotten, giving double the links. Use the 'each cable has two ends' explanation.
say: 'Star: one centre, one cable each, one point of failure.'
'Mesh: many links, many routes, much money.'
'n times n minus one, over two. Say it before you draw it.'
teacher.skip: Try 3 can go if space is tight; Try 1 and Try 5 carry the exam skill (drawing and justifying).
differentiation: Support: give dotted-outline templates for the star and the four-node mesh to trace and label before drawing freehand.
Stretch: in Try 2, write a function that checks whether a partial mesh (given as a list of links) still connects every device when one named link is removed.
